arXiv:0901.3859v1 [math.PR] 24 Jan 2009

A phase diagram for a stochastic reaction diffusion system.

Carl Mueller Affiliation: and    University of Rochester Affiliation: Roger Tribe, Warwick University.
Abstract

In this paper a stochastic reaction diffusion system is considered, which models the spread of a finite population reacting with a non-renewable resource in the presence of individual based noise. A two-parameter phase diagram is established to describe the large time evolution, distinguishing between certain death or possible life of the population.

KEYWORDS: Stochastic PDE; Dawson-Watanabe process; exit measures; phase diagram; oriented percolation.

1 Introduction

1.1 Statement of results

In this paper we study the stochastic reaction diffusion system on RdR^{d}, for d≤3d\leq 3,

{∂tu=Δ​u+β​u​v−γ​u+u​W˙,∂tv=−u​v.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u+\beta uv-\gamma u+\sqrt{u}\,\dot{W},\\ \partial_{t}v=-uv.\end{array}\right. (1.1)

One interpretation for this equation is that the solution u≥0u\geq 0 describes the distribution of a population on RdR^{d} at times t≥0t\geq 0 and that v≥0v\geq 0 is the density of a nutrient gradually used up by the population. The noise WW is a space-time white noise, and the multiplicative factor u\sqrt{u} models ‘individual based’ noise. This noise arises in situations where each individual in the population contributes independently to the noise, so that the variance of the noise is proportional to the population density. In dimensions d≤3d\leq 3, linear scaling reduces the number of possible parameters to two. We have chosen to take the diffusion coefficient, the rate at which the nutrient is used, and the noise coefficient all to be one, leaving two parameters β,γ≥0\beta,\gamma\geq 0, which we think of as a reaction rate and a death rate.

The main results concern the long time behaviour of solutions. Without noise there are travelling wave solutions and it is expected that sufficient noise can destroy these waves. For our description of the long time behaviour, we take an initial condition u0=μu_{0}=\mu in ℳ⁡(Rd)\mathcal{M}(R^{d}), the space of finite measures in RdR^{d}, and an initial nutrient level v0​(x)v_{0}(x) taking a constant value which, by scaling again, we have taken to be 11. We say that certain death occurs for the parameters values β,γ\beta,\gamma if

P[ut=0for larget]=1P\left[u_{t}=0\;\mbox{for large}\;t\right]=1 for any initial condition μ∈ℳ⁡(Rd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(R^{d}) and v0=1v_{0}=1.

We say that possible life occurs for the parameter values β,γ\beta,\gamma if

P[ut≠0for allt]>0P\left[u_{t}\not=0\;\mbox{for all}\;t\right]>0 for any non-zero initial condition μ∈ℳ⁡(Rd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(R^{d}) and v0=1v_{0}=1.

The main results of the paper describe a phase diagram for the parameter values β,γ\beta,\gamma at which certain death or possible life occur.

Theorem 1.

Consider solutions to (1.1) with initial condition v0=1v_{0}=1. Then for any values of the parameters β,γ≥0\beta,\gamma\geq 0 either possible life or certain death occurs.

  • •

    When d=3, there exists a non-decreasing function β→Ψ⁡(β)∈(0,β)\beta\to\Psi(\beta)\in(0,\beta) so that when 0≤γ<Ψ⁡(β)0\leq\gamma<\Psi(\beta) possible life occurs and when γ>Ψ⁡(β)\gamma>\Psi(\beta) certain death occurs. Moreover

    0<lim infβ→0β−2​Ψ​(β)≤lim supβ→0β−2​Ψ​(β)<∞,0<\liminf_{\beta\to 0}\beta^{-2}\Psi(\beta)\leq\limsup_{\beta\to 0}\beta^{-2}\Psi(\beta)<\infty,
  • •

    When d=2 there exists a critical curve β→Ψ⁡(β)∈[0,β)\beta\to\Psi(\beta)\in[0,\beta) as in dimension d=3d=3 (but allowing the possibility that Ψ⁡(β)=0\Psi(\beta)=0 for small β\beta).

  • •

    When d=1 certain death occurs for any γ,β≥0\gamma,\beta\geq 0.

Remarks

1. The estimates in the paper imply certain bounds on the critical curve. In section 6.3 we show that Ψ⁡(β)/β→1\Psi(\beta)/\beta\to 1 as β→∞\beta\to\infty. This asymptotic is not sharp, and the correct large β\beta asymptotic is, we believe, β−Ψ(β)∼β−2/(6−d)\beta-\Psi(\beta)\sim\beta^{-2/(6-d)}. The remarks in section 6.3 indicate that a certain improved spatial Markov property is required to establish these asymptotics, and the details are left to a subsequent paper. Many other questions remain, such as regularity of Ψ\Psi and the behaviour on the critical curve. Most importantly perhaps, we do not know the small β\beta behaviour in d=2d=2, though we conjecture (see section 7.3) that there is certain death for γ=0\gamma=0 and small enough β\beta.

2. The possible life behaviour is not an example of global coexistence of two species, for locally either the population utu_{t} becomes extinct or the nutrient levels converge to zero (see Lemma 9). Rather one expects the process to live on a moving front travelling through space, and behind this moving front the nutrient is used up and the process dies away. It is therefore more analogous to the weak survival results for the contact process on a homogeneous tree (see [8] section I.4).

3. A key difficulty in dealing with many reaction diffusion systems is the lack of pathwise comparison results (which were crucial to the arguments for the scalar equation studied in [9]). For example if two solutions u,u~u,\tilde{u} satisfy u0≤u~0u_{0}\leq\tilde{u}_{0} one should not expect that ut≤u~tu_{t}\leq\tilde{u}_{t} for t>0t>0. To replace these arguments, the key new method in this paper is the use of comparison results for the total occupation measure ∫0∞ut​𝑑t\int^{\infty}_{0}u_{t}dt and total exit measure u∞∂Du_{\infty}^{\partial D} of solutions on a domain DD. Some intuition behind this is given in section 1.2.

4. Using scaling (as in Lemma 3) one can investigate the dependence on other parameters. For example the equation

{∂tu=Δ​u+u​v−γ0​u+σ​u​W˙,∂tv=−uv,v0=1.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u+uv-\gamma_{0}u+\sqrt{\sigma u}\,\dot{W},\\ \partial_{t}v=-uv,\quad v_{0}=1.\end{array}\right.

can be reduced to the standard form (1.1), by a linear change of variables, with the parameters becoming γ=γ0σ−2/(4−d)\gamma=\gamma_{0}\sigma^{-2/(4-d)} and β=σ−2/(4−d)\beta=\sigma^{-2/(4-d)}. The main theorem shows that possible life occurs, for example when d=3d=3, if 0≤γ0<Φ⁡(σ)0\leq\gamma_{0}<\Phi(\sigma) for some Φ:(0,∞)→(0,1)\Phi:(0,\infty)\to(0,1) and satisfying limσ→0Φ⁡(σ)=1\lim_{\sigma\to 0}\Phi(\sigma)=1 and limσ→∞Φ⁡(σ)=0\lim_{\sigma\to\infty}\Phi(\sigma)=0 at certain rates. One reason for choosing β,γ\beta,\gamma as our parameters is that we have natural monotonicity in these parameters which is unclear for other choices - for example we do not know if Φ\Phi is decreasing.

5. One can investigate, via phase plane methods, the possibility of travelling waves for the corresponding deterministic system ∂tu=Δ​u+u​v−γ​u,∂tv=−u​v\partial_{t}u=\Delta u+uv-\gamma u,\;\partial_{t}v=-uv with v0=1v_{0}=1. (With no noise term and β>0\beta>0 we can remove one more parameter by linear scaling, leaving only γ≥0\gamma\geq 0.) We require γ≤1\gamma\leq 1, else the death term exceeds the reaction term resulting in death. Fix k∈Rdk\in R^{d} with |k|=1|k|=1. Looking for a travelling wave solution of the form ut​(x)=U⁡((x⋅k)−c​t),vt​(x)=V⁡((x⋅k)−c​t)u_{t}(x)=U((x\cdot k)-ct),\,v_{t}(x)=V((x\cdot k)-ct) with c>0c>0, we set W=U′W=U^{\prime} to obtain the first order system

U′=W,V′=1c​U​V,W′=γ​U−c​W−U​V.U^{\prime}=W,\quad V^{\prime}=\frac{1}{c}UV,\quad W^{\prime}=\gamma U-cW-UV.

The steady states are (U,V,W)=(0,a,0)(U,V,W)=(0,a,0) for any aa. By scaling we assume the untouched nutrient level is 11 and seek a path in phase space connecting (0,0,0)(0,0,0) to (0,1,0)(0,1,0), so that uu is a travelling ‘hump’, behind the wave the nutrient is used up and ahead it is untouched. Linearizing around (0,0,0)(0,0,0) we find the eigenvalues satisfy λ=0\lambda=0 or λ2+c​λ−γ=0\lambda^{2}+c\lambda-\gamma=0. So for any γ>0\gamma>0 we have real eigenvalues λ1<0=λ2<λ3\lambda_{1}<0=\lambda_{2}<\lambda_{3}. Linearizing around (0,1,0)(0,1,0) we obtain λ=0\lambda=0 or λ2+c​λ+(1−γ)=0\lambda^{2}+c\lambda+(1-\gamma)=0. For γ<1\gamma<1 we get λ1<λ2<0=λ3\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}<0=\lambda_{3} when c2≥4​(1−γ)c^{2}\geq 4(1-\gamma). Complex roots, which imply the impossibility of a (non-negative) travelling wave, occur when c2<4​(1−γ)c^{2}<4(1-\gamma). The equations are three dimensional and degenerate and we have not done a rigorous analysis. Based on the above local picture, the following seems the reasonable best guess: there is a unique path connecting (0,0,0)(0,0,0) to (0,1,0)(0,1,0) which stays in the good region U,V>0U,V>0 precisely if c2≥4​(1−γ)c^{2}\geq 4(1-\gamma) and hence a travelling wave for all γ<1\gamma<1 and with speeds greater than or equal to 2​1−γ2\sqrt{1-\gamma}. The main result supports the conjecture that the deterministic travelling waves are stable to small enough individual based noise noise in dimensions d=2,3d=2,3.

1.2 A description of key techniques and the layout of the paper

In this section we explain some of the intuition and tools used in the proofs, emphasising the new ideas.

When β=0\beta=0, solutions uu to (1.1) are Dawson-Watanabe processes with underlying Brownian motion and mass annihilation at rate γ\gamma. In dimensions d≥2d\geq 2, Dawson-Watanabe processes are singular measures (ut(dx):t≥0)(u_{t}(dx):t\geq 0). However, as shown by Sugitani [13], when d≤3d\leq 3 the occupation measures ∫stur​𝑑r\int^{t}_{s}u_{r}dr are absolutely continuous with repsect to Lebesgue measure, with densities u⁡(s,t,x)u(s,t,x). This will remain true for for solutions to (1.1) and hence the the formal solution vt​(x)=v0​(x)​exp⁡(−u⁡(0,t,x))v_{t}(x)=v_{0}(x)\exp(-u(0,t,x)) will make sense as a function. Using this idea, we construct solutions to (1.1) in d≤3d\leq 3 by a change of measure starting from a Dawson-Watanabe process; a reverse argument yields uniqueness in law of solutions.

The results on possible life use a construction of a supercritical oriented percolation process, coupled to a solution of (1.1), so that if the oriented percolation survives so too does the solution. The use of an embedded oriented percolation to show survival was first developed for interacting particle systems (see Durrett [4] for many examples). Similar methods have been used before by the authors to establish a one-parameter phase transition for a noisy version of the KPP equation [9]. The results on certain death in dimensions d≥2d\geq 2 are simpler, and the background idea is a comparison with a subcritical branching process (for which simple moment estimates show death).

When possible life occurs, one expects that the process lives on a front propagating with asymptotically linear speed. Noisy oscillations around this linear speed mean that it is not possible to predict exactly where in space, at a given time tt, to look for the living part of the solution (that is where it is in the process of exploiting the nutrient). This leads to the wish to apply the percolation comparison in space at random times. To overcome this technical problem, we freeze the process at random stopping times, by means of exit measures. The exit measures can be constructed by solving (1.1) on a domain DD with Dirichlet boundary conditions and measuring the total flux of mass out of the boundary of the domain. Suitable comparison results do hold for this model, not for ut​(d​x)u_{t}(dx) but for the total exit measures u∞∂D​(d​x)u^{\partial D}_{\infty}(dx). For example if u0​(d​x)u_{0}(dx) and u~0​(d​x)\tilde{u}_{0}(dx) are supported inside DD and u0​(d​x)≤u~0​(d​x)u_{0}(dx)\leq\tilde{u}_{0}(dx), then one can construct solutions for which u∞∂D​(d​x)≤u~∞∂D​(d​x)u^{\partial D}_{\infty}(dx)\leq\tilde{u}^{\partial D}_{\infty}(dx). It turns out that the total exit measures are stochastically monotone both in the initial conditions and in the parameters β,γ\beta,\gamma. A spatial Markov property, analogous to that found for Dawson-Watanabe processes by Dynkin in [5], shows that exit measures can be constructed iteratively on larger and larger domains, and is used to set up the percolation comparison. It is this spatial Markov property especially, that means the use of the special form of noise u​W˙\sqrt{u}\dot{W} is needed for our methods.

Intuition as to why comparison results hold for the total exit measures is easiest for particle approximations to (1.1), where population particles may react with nutrient particles leading to death of a nutrient particle and the creation of extra population particles. The total exit measures do not depend on the time at which particles hit the exit of the domain DD. It does not affect the final level of the nutrient v∞​(x)v_{\infty}(x) if we change the order that particles pass through position xx. For example, we may think of the initial mass u~0​(d​x)\tilde{u}_{0}(dx) as being composed of blue particles, identical to those from u0​(d​x)u_{0}(dx) and some extra red particles represented by u~0​(d​x)−u0​(d​x)\tilde{u}_{0}(dx)-u_{0}(dx). We freeze the extra red particles until all the blue particles have died or are frozen on ∂D\partial D. Then we may run the red particles through whatever is left of the nutrient, but this can only lead to a larger exit measure. The reader may wish to draw a diagram illustrating the possible interactions for the simplest non-trivial case of two population particles and a single nutrient particle - it was such a diagram that initiated this work.

Layout. In section 2 we state the existence, uniqueness and comparison results for occupation and exit measures. Section 3 contains the change of measure arguments needed for the proof of existence and uniqueness, and the proof of the existence of a critical curve Ψ⁡(β)\Psi(\beta). Approximations to solutions, using a discretized nutrient, are given in section 4, together with tightness and convergence results. Comparison results for the approximations are established in section 5 together with the weak convergence arguments allowing us to pass to the continuous limit. However, the arguments for life (in section 6) and death (in section 7) can be read after the statement of the comparison results in section 2.

2 Statements of existence, uniqueness and comparison results

2.1 Definition of solutions

We need to consider solutions to (1.1) on domains DD. Throughout the paper our domains are taken to be either (i) connected open sets with smooth boundary; or (ii) open boxes, that is of the form D=∏i(ai,bi)D=\prod_{i}(a_{i},b_{i}) for −∞≤ai<bi≤∞-\infty\leq a_{i}<b_{i}\leq\infty. This restriction allows us to quote estimates on the Green’s functions for the domain. Moreover, boxes will be all that we need for the blocking arguments in sections 6 and 7. We will look for solutions with zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, that is where the population is killed on reaching the boundary. This will be encoded by the test functions for the martingale problem below. We let Cbk​(D¯)C^{k}_{b}(\overline{D}) be the space of kk-times continuously differentiable functions ϕ:D→R\phi:D\to R for which ϕ\phi and its derivatives can be extended to be continuous bounded functions on the closure D¯\overline{D}. Let C02​(D¯)C^{2}_{0}(\overline{D}) be the subset of those ϕ∈Cb2​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D}) for which ϕ=0\phi=0 on ∂D\partial D. Note that solutions on D=RdD=R^{d} are a special case of the definition below, and in this case C02​(D¯)C^{2}_{0}(\overline{D}) reduces to the space of bounded functions with two bounded continuous derivatives.

    E[h(uτ+⋅)|ℱτ]=Quτ,v0​exp⁡(−u⁡(0,τ))D,β,γ[h(U⋅)]P a.s,E\left[h(u_{\tau+\cdot})|\mathcal{F}_{\tau}\right]=Q_{u_{\tau},v_{0}\exp(-u(0,\tau))}^{D,\beta,\gamma}\left[h(U_{\cdot})\right]\qquad\mbox{$P$ a.s,}

    for all bounded measurable h:C⁡([0,∞),ℳ⁡(D))→Rh:C([0,\infty),\mathcal{M}(D))\to R.

We note one consequence of these results: using part (iii), whenever (u,v)(u,v) is a solution we may replace vv by the process v0​(x)​exp⁡(−u⁡(0,t,x))v_{0}(x)\exp(-u(0,t,x)) and it will still be a solution.

The following scaling lemma will be very useful in allowing us to transfer large or small parameters to terms in the equations that are convenient. We find our intuition stronger when working in regimes with small or large values of parameters, rather than small or large space and time scales. This lemma allows us to transfer between these two regimes.

Lemma 3.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a solution to (1.1) on DD. For a,b,c,e>0a,b,c,e>0 define

{∂tu~=bc2​Δ​u~+b​βe​u~​v~−b​γ​u~+a​bcd​u~​W˙,∂tv~=−ba​u~​v~.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\tilde{u}=\frac{b}{c^{2}}\Delta\tilde{u}+\frac{b\beta}{e}\tilde{u}\,\tilde{v}-b\gamma\tilde{u}+\sqrt{\frac{ab}{c^{d}}\tilde{u}}\,\dot{W},\\ \partial_{t}\tilde{v}=-\frac{b}{a}\tilde{u}\,\tilde{v}.\end{array}\right.

The equation for (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) follows immediately by scaling the martingale problem (2.1,2.2). 2.2 Decomposition results for the total occupation and exit measures

Notation. For a solution (u,v)(u,v) to (1.1) we write u[s,t]u_{[s,t]} for the occupation measure ∫stur​𝑑r\int^{t}_{s}u_{r}dr (so that u[s,t]​(d​x)=u⁡(s,t,x)​d​xu_{[s,t]}(dx)=u(s,t,x)dx PP a.s.) and write

for the total occupation measure on DD and its density, and for the total exit measure on ∂D\partial D.

The lemmas below are stated under the restriction that DD is bounded, which implies (see section 3.3) that the total occupation and exit measures are almost surely finite. The first lemma describes the monotonicity of the total occupation and exit measures with respect to the initial conditions (μ,f)(\mu,f). We write =𝒟\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}}}{{=}} for equality in distribution.

(ii) (u−,v−)(u^{-},v^{-}) is a solution with initial conditions (μ,f−)(\mu,f^{-}) and, conditional on σ​{u−}\sigma\{u^{-}\}, the process (u+,v+)(u^{+},v^{+}) is a solution with initial conditions u0+=β​f+​(1−exp⁡(−u−​(0,∞)))​d​xu^{+}_{0}=\beta f^{+}(1-\exp(-u^{-}(0,\infty)))\,dx and v0+=f​exp⁡(−u−​(0,∞))v^{+}_{0}=f\exp(-u^{-}(0,\infty)).

The next lemma shows monotonicity in the parameters β\beta, γ\gamma.

Lemma 5.

Fix a bounded domain DD, and parameter values β=β−+β+\beta=\beta^{-}+\beta^{+} and γ−=γ+γ+\gamma^{-}=\gamma+\gamma^{+}. The law of the total occupation and exit measures of a solution (u,v)(u,v) to (1.1) on a bounded domain DD with initial conditions (μ,f)(\mu,f) and parameter values (β,γ)(\beta,\gamma) can be decomposed as in (2.5) in either of the following two ways:

A special case of the Lemma 5 (i) will be particularly useful. The total exit measure can be built up in two stages: first run a process with β=0\beta=0 (which is the well understood Dawson-Watanabe process) and then run a second solution started with the mass that the nutrient would have produced from the first process.

The following simpler comparison will often be useful. It states, roughly, that if we convert some of the nutrient available into the equivalent amount of initial mass at time zero then we obtain a healthier process, in the sense of stochastic ordering.

Lemma 6.

Fix a bounded domain DD and initial conditions μ\mu and f,gf,g. Let (u,v)(u,v) and (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) be solutions to (1.1) on DD with initial conditions (μ,f+g)(\mu,f+g) and (μ+β​g​d​x,f)(\mu+\beta g\,dx,f) respectively. Then for any bounded measurable F:ℳ⁡(D)×ℳ⁡(∂D)→RF:\mathcal{M}(D)\times\mathcal{M}(\partial D)\to R that is non-decreasing in both variables

E⁡[F⁡(u[0,∞),u∞∂D)]≤E⁡[F⁡(u~[0,∞),u~∞∂D)].E[F(u_{[0,\infty)},u^{\partial D}_{\infty})]\leq E[F(\tilde{u}_{[0,\infty)},\tilde{u}^{\partial D}_{\infty})].

The final lemma is a spatial Markov property, analogous to that known for Dawson-Watanabe processes. We choose two domains D−⊆D+D^{-}\subseteq D^{+}. We allow the boundaries ∂D−\partial D^{-} and ∂D+\partial D^{+} to intersect, but we need this intersection not to be too complicated, and for this we ask that

(∂D−∩∂D+)∩(∂D−∖∂D+)¯(\partial D^{-}\cap\partial D^{+})\cap\overline{(\partial D^{-}\setminus\partial D^{+})} has surface measure zero in ∂D−\partial D^{-}. (2.6)

This is satisfied for example if both domains are boxes. We write μ|A\mu|_{A} for the restriction of a measure μ\mu to a set AA.

Lemma 7.

Fix bounded domains D−⊆D+D^{-}\subseteq D^{+} satisfying (2.6). Suppose (u,v)(u,v) is a solution to (1.1) on D+D^{+} started at (μ,f)(\mu,f). Then the law of the total occupation and exit measures satisfies

(u[0,∞),u∞∂D+)=𝒟(u[0,∞)−+u[0,∞)+,u∞∂D−,−|∂D++u∞∂D+,+)\left(u_{[0,\infty)},u^{\partial D^{+}}_{\infty}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}}}{{=}}\left(u^{-}_{[0,\infty)}+u^{+}_{[0,\infty)},u^{\partial D^{-},-}_{\infty}|_{\partial D^{+}}+u^{\partial D^{+},+}_{\infty}\right)

where (u−,v−)(u^{-},v^{-}) is a solution to (1.1) on D−D^{-} with initial conditions (μ​I​(D−),f​I​(D−))(\mu I(D^{-}),fI(D^{-})) and, conditional on σ​{u−}\sigma\{u^{-}\}, the process (u+,v+)(u^{+},v^{+}) is a solution on D+D^{+} with initial conditions

u0+=u∞∂D−,−|D++μ​I​(D+∖D−)andv0+=v∞−​I​(D−)+f​I​(D+∖D−).u^{+}_{0}=u^{\partial D^{-},-}_{\infty}|_{D^{+}}+\mu I(D^{+}\setminus D^{-})\quad\mbox{and}\quad v^{+}_{0}=v^{-}_{\infty}I(D^{-})+fI(D^{+}\setminus D^{-}).

Remark. As indicated in the introduction, these lemmas will be proved for discretized approximations to solutions, where the nutrient is used up in finitely many steps, and then via a passage to the limit. We spent considerable energy trying to find a proof using the continuum equation (1.1) directly. Approaches using a change of measure (since the lemmas are easy to prove for a Dawson-Watanabe process) typically failed because the decomposition (2.5) holds only for the total occupation and exit measures and fails for these measures at times t<∞t<\infty. Another approach, using Laplace functionals, is sketched in remark (b) of section 3.1. On the other hand, we found the discretized approximations, in particular particle pictures, were the easiest testing ground for exploring possible extensions of these results to other models.

3 Change of measure arguments

In section 3.1 we review some results on Dawson-Watanabe processes and indicate when these imply estimates for solutions of (1.1). Section 3.2 gives the proof of Theorem 2, and section 3.3 contains the proof of the existence of the critical curve Ψ⁡(β)\Psi(\beta).

3.1 Results from Dawson-Watanabe processes

A Dawson-Watanabe process, with underlying Brownian spatial motion, killed at the exit of a domain DD, and with a (deterministic) bounded, measurable mass annihilation/creation rate η:D→R\eta:D\to R, is the solution on DD, in the same sense as in section 2.1, to the equation

∂tu=Δ​u−η​u+u​W˙.\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\eta u+\sqrt{u}\,\dot{W}. (3.1)

We shall abbreviate Dawson-Watanabe processes as DW processes. In the case η⁡(x)=γ∈R\eta(x)=\gamma\in R is constant we will call the process a DW(D,γD,\gamma) process. We describe below some results for DW processes that we shall need, and we mostly indicate where to find the proofs, or how to adapt them, from the literature. The surveys by Perkins [10] and Dawson [2] are our main sources. However, we give proofs for some of the results on exit measures, that are perhaps not in the literature, at the end of this subsection.

A number of the estimates (for example moment bounds, estimates on the speed of the support, estimates on the extinction probability) also hold for solutions to (1.1). One way to see this is to set up a pathwise coupling for (u,v)(u,v) a solution to (1.1) on DD so that ut(1)≤ut≤ut(2)u^{(1)}_{t}\leq u_{t}\leq u^{(2)}_{t} where u(1)u^{(1)} is a DW(D,γD,\gamma) process and u(2)u^{(2)} is a DW(D,γ−βD,\gamma-\beta) process. We do not go through the steps to construct this coupling since, as we indicate below, the proofs of the desired estimates are typically based on stochastic calculus and are easily adapted to follow from the martingale problem for solutions to (1.1).

1. Martingale problems. We quickly repeat here the martingale problem definition for solutions. A continuous, adapted ℳ⁡(D)\mathcal{M}(D) valued process uu, on some filtered space (Ω,(ℱt),ℱ,P)(\Omega,(\mathcal{F}_{t}),\mathcal{F},P), is a solution to (3.1) if for ϕ∈C02​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{0}(\overline{D})

ut​(ϕ)=u0​(ϕ)+∫0tus​(Δ​ϕ−η​ϕ)​𝑑s+mt​(ϕ),P a.s.u_{t}(\phi)=u_{0}(\phi)+\int^{t}_{0}u_{s}\left(\Delta\phi-\eta\phi\right)ds+m_{t}(\phi),\quad\mbox{$P$ a.s.} (3.2)

where mt​(ϕ)m_{t}(\phi) is a continuous (ℱt)(\mathcal{F}_{t}) local martingale with quadratic variation [m⁡(ϕ)]t=∫0tus​(ϕ2)​𝑑s[m(\phi)]_{t}=\int^{t}_{0}u_{s}(\phi^{2})ds almost surely. Solutions, starting from μ∈ℳ⁡(D)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(D), exist and are unique in law on C⁡([0,∞),ℳ⁡(D))C([0,\infty),\mathcal{M}(D)). Furthermore, for any solution there will exist an adapted process (ut∂D)(u^{\partial D}_{t}) with non-decreasing continuous paths in ℳ⁡(∂D)\mathcal{M}(\partial D), called the exit measure process, so that for ϕ∈Cb2​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D})

ut​(ϕ)=u0​(ϕ)+∫0tus​(Δ​ϕ−η​ϕ)​𝑑s−ut∂D​(ϕ)+mt​(ϕ),P a.s.u_{t}(\phi)=u_{0}(\phi)+\int^{t}_{0}u_{s}\left(\Delta\phi-\eta\phi\right)ds-u^{\partial D}_{t}(\phi)+m_{t}(\phi),\quad\mbox{$P$ a.s.} (3.3)

where mt​(ϕ)m_{t}(\phi) is a continuous local martingale with variation as before. The almost sure linearity mt​(ϕ+ψ)=mt​(ϕ)+mt​(ψ)m_{t}(\phi+\psi)=m_{t}(\phi)+m_{t}(\psi), implies that if ϕn∈C02​(D¯)\phi_{n}\in C^{2}_{0}(\overline{D}) converge bounded pointwise to ϕ∈Cb2​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D}) then mt​(ϕn)→mt​(ϕ)m_{t}(\phi_{n})\to m_{t}(\phi) in probability (since [m⁡(ϕ−ϕn)]t→0[m(\phi-\phi_{n})]_{t}\to 0). Now (3.2) and (3.3) imply that ut∂D​(ϕ)u_{t}^{\partial D}(\phi) is measurable function of the path (us:s≤t)(u_{s}:s\leq t). Choose is a countable family (ϕk)k=1,…(\phi_{k})_{k=1,\ldots} in Cb2​(D¯)C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D}) so that the map μ→(μ⁡(ϕk))k=1,…\mu\to(\mu(\phi_{k}))_{k=1,\ldots} is a continuous injection from ℳ⁡(∂D)\mathcal{M}(\partial D) into R∞R^{\infty} (with the topology of uniform convergence on compacts). Using the measurable inverse of this map, one one can construct a measurable map Rt:C⁡([0,t],ℳ⁡(D))→ℳ⁡(∂D)R_{t}:C([0,t],\mathcal{M}(D))\to\mathcal{M}(\partial D) so that

ut∂D=Rt​({us:s≤t})P a.s.u^{\partial D}_{t}=R_{t}(\{u_{s}:s\leq t\})\quad\mbox{$P$ a.s.} (3.4)

These maps show that the law of (u,u∂D)(u,u^{\partial D}) on ΩD\Omega_{D} is determined by the law of uu on C⁡([0,∞),ℳ⁡(D))C([0,\infty),\mathcal{M}(D)). Also, for any DW process on DD, the exit measure process can be constructed by using the maps RtR_{t} and then regularizing the path over the rationals.

Notation. We denote by QμD,ηQ^{D,\eta}_{\mu} the law on ΩD\Omega_{D} of a DW process and its exit measure (u,u∂D)(u,u^{\partial D}) on DD, with mass annihilation/creation rate η\eta as above, and starting at μ∈ℳ⁡(D)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(D). We write QμD,γQ^{D,\gamma}_{\mu} in the case that η⁡(x)=γ\eta(x)=\gamma.

The map μ→QμD,η​(B)\mu\to Q^{D,\eta}_{\mu}(B) is measurable for any Borel B⊆ΩDB\subseteq\Omega_{D}; furthermore the family of laws (QμD,η:μ∈ℳ(D))(Q^{D,\eta}_{\mu}:\mu\in\mathcal{M}(D)) form a strong Markov family in that for any solution uu defined on (Ω,(ℱt),ℱ,P)(\Omega,(\mathcal{F}_{t}),\mathcal{F},P), and any finite (ℱt)(\mathcal{F}_{t}) stopping time τ\tau,

E[h(uτ+⋅)|ℱτ]=QuτD,η[h(U⋅)]P a.s,E\left[h(u_{\tau+\cdot})|\mathcal{F}_{\tau}\right]=Q_{u_{\tau}}^{D,\eta}\left[h(U_{\cdot})\right]\qquad\mbox{$P$ a.s,}

Since the exit measures ut∂Du^{\partial D}_{t} are non-decreasing, they induce a unique measure d​ut∂D​(d​x)du^{\partial D}_{t}(dx) on [0,∞)×∂D[0,\infty)\times\partial D characterized by the measure of the rectangles (s,t]×A(s,t]\times A being ut∂D​(A)−us∂D​(A)u^{\partial D}_{t}(A)-u_{s}^{\partial D}(A). ut​(ϕt)=u0​(ϕ0)+∫0tus​(Δ​ϕs+ϕ˙s−η​ϕs)​𝑑s−∫0td​us∂D​(ϕs)+mt​(ϕ)P a.s.u_{t}(\phi_{t})=u_{0}(\phi_{0})+\int^{t}_{0}u_{s}\left(\Delta\phi_{s}+\dot{\phi}_{s}-\eta\phi_{s}\right)ds-\int^{t}_{0}du_{s}^{\partial D}(\phi_{s})+m_{t}(\phi)\quad\mbox{$P$ a.s.} (3.5)

This follows using easier versions of the arguments in [10] Proposition II.5.7. Moreover, the analogous extension works for solutions to (1.1).

When the domain DD is a box the associated p.d.e.’s have unique solutions that are smooth inside DD and continuous on D¯\overline{D}, and the formulae for the Laplace functionals still hold, and can be established by an approximation argument. Indeed, one concrete way to do this is to suppose, without loss, that DD contains the origin and to replace the test functions above by ϕt​(x/(1+ϵ))\phi_{t}(x/(1+\epsilon)) and ϕ⁡(x/(1+ϵ)CLOSE\phi(x/(1+\epsilon), which are smooth in D¯\overline{D}.

Remark (a). From the pde viewpoint, it is natural to use (3.3) as a means of characterizing the exit measures t→ut∂D​(d​x)t\to u^{\partial D}_{t}(dx), that is purely as exit fluxes (as is suggested in [11]). Construct the martingale measure m⁡(d​x,d​s)m(dx,ds) from a DW(D,γD,\gamma) process. Then for smooth h:∂D→Rh:\partial D\to R we may uniquely find ϕh∈Cb2​(D¯)\phi^{h}\in C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D}) solving the Dirichlet problem Δ​ϕh=0\Delta\phi^{h}=0 on DD and ϕh=h\phi^{h}=h on ∂D\partial D. Use the formula (3.3) with the test function ϕh\phi^{h} to define a continuous path t→ut∂D​(h)t\to u^{\partial D}_{t}(h) (although we have yet to establish that the values ut∂D​(h)u^{\partial D}_{t}(h) arise from a measure ut∂Du^{\partial D}_{t} on ∂D\partial D). By adding the decompositions (3.3) for ϕg\phi^{g} and ϕh\phi^{h} we find that ut∂D​(g+h)=ut∂D​(g)+ut∂D​(h)u^{\partial D}_{t}(g+h)=u^{\partial D}_{t}(g)+u^{\partial D}_{t}(h) almost surely. For ϕ∈Cb2​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D}) with ϕ=h\phi=h on ∂D\partial D, the decomposition (3.3) holds by adding the decompositions for ϕh\phi^{h} and ϕ−ϕh\phi-\phi^{h}. Then the first moment bounds allow the decompositions to be extended to time dependent test functions ϕ⁡(t,x)\phi(t,x) as above. In particular we find, for h≥0h\geq 0, that E⁡[exp⁡(−λ​ut∂D​(h))]≤exp⁡(−μ⁡(ϕt))E[\exp(-\lambda u^{\partial D}_{t}(h))]\leq\exp(-\mu(\phi_{t})) where ∂tϕ=Δ​ϕ−γ​ϕ−ϕ22\partial_{t}\phi=\Delta\phi-\gamma\phi-\frac{\phi^{2}}{2} on DD, and ϕt=λ​h\phi_{t}=\lambda h on ∂D\partial D, and ϕ0=0\phi_{0}=0. Finally the Markov property implies that ut∂D−us∂Du^{\partial D}_{t}-u^{\partial D}_{s} is non-negative and hence the paths of ut∂Du^{\partial D}_{t} are non-decreasing.

Remark (b). Mimicking the calculus that leads to the Laplace functional above, one can show that for solutions to (1.1) that

Sugitani [13] studied the occupation measure under the law QμRd,0Q^{R^{d},0}_{\mu} of a DW process on RdR^{d}. His main result extends to our processes on more general domains, and with bounded annihilation/creation rates, as follows: QμD,ηQ^{D,\eta}_{\mu} almost surely, the process (s,t,x)→U⁡(s,t,x)(s,t,x)\to U(s,t,x) is continuous over 0<s≤t,x∈D0<s\leq t,\,x\in D, and x→U⁡(s,t,x)x\to U(s,t,x) acts as a density for U[s,t]U_{[s,t]}. One way of representing the density is via a Green’s function formula, as follows. Let G[0,t]D,x=∫0tGsD,x​𝑑sG^{D,x}_{[0,t]}=\int^{t}_{0}G^{D,x}_{s}ds and G[0,t]D,γ,x=∫0tGsD,γ,x​𝑑sG^{D,\gamma,x}_{[0,t]}=\int^{t}_{0}G^{D,\gamma,x}_{s}ds. Then, for a fixed t>δ>0t>\delta>0 and x∈Dx\in D,

U⁡(δ,t,x)=Uδ​(G[0,t−δ]D,x)+∫δt∫DG[0,t−s]D,x​(z)​(−η⁡(z)​Us​(𝑑z)​𝑑s+M⁡(𝑑z,𝑑s))QμD,η a.s.U(\delta,t,x)=U_{\delta}(G^{D,x}_{[0,t-\delta]})+\int^{t}_{\delta}\int_{D}G^{D,x}_{[0,t-s]}(z)(-\eta(z)U_{s}(dz)ds+M(dz,ds))\quad\mbox{$Q^{D,\eta}_{\mu}$ a.s.} (3.19)

where M⁡(d​z,d​s)M(dz,ds) is the martingale measure associated to UU. Moreover, for k∈Nk\in N,

QμD,η​[U​(δ,t,x)k]≤C⁡(k,δ,μ,‖η‖∞,T)for all x∈D,t∈[δ,T].Q^{D,\eta}_{\mu}[U(\delta,t,x)^{k}]\leq C(k,\delta,\mu,\|\eta\|_{\infty},T)\quad\mbox{for all $x\in D,t\in[\delta,T]$.} (3.20)

When the initial condition is more one may take δ=0\delta=0 in (3.19), and indeed this is the case if μ\mu has a bounded density. In particular, when μ⁡(d​x)=β​d​x\mu(dx)=\beta dx we have, for k∈Nk\in N,

Qβ​d​xD,η​[U​(0,t,x)k]≤C⁡(k,β,‖η‖∞,T)for all x∈D,t∈[0,T].Q^{D,\eta}_{\beta dx}[U(0,t,x)^{k}]\leq C(k,\beta,\|\eta\|_{\infty},T)\quad\mbox{for all $x\in D,t\in[0,T]$.} (3.21)

It is not hard to extend Sugitani’s proof of the representation formula to hold for domains DD and with annihilation/creation terms, and also to bound the moments (inductively in kk). Sugitani’s proof of continuity is via Kolmogorov’s continuity criterion and moments of increments. We omit the details since we will follow Sugitani’s arguments to establish a similar increment estimates for approximations to solutions in section 4.2, and some of the key steps are illustrated there.

6. A construction of the exit measure process and the spatial Markov property. A convenient way to construct the exit measure processes was developed in Perkins [11], which will be useful in our proof of a coupling version of the spatial Markov property lemma below. This exploits a historical DW process, which is a process of random measures on the space of paths, where intuitively the paths trace the positions of the ancestors of the particles in a DW process. To explain the construction, we recall some notation from [11] for the historical Brownian DW process (which is only required in this one subsection): on the path space C⁡([0,∞),Rd)C([0,\infty),R^{d}) let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the Borel σ\sigma-field and (𝒞t)(\mathcal{C}_{t}) the canonical filtration; ℳ⁡(C)\mathcal{M}(C) is the space of finite measures on C⁡([0,∞),Rd)C([0,\infty),R^{d}) with the topology of weak convergence; on ΩH=C⁡([0,∞),ℳ⁡(C))\Omega_{H}=C([0,\infty),\mathcal{M}(C)) let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the Borel sets and (Ht)(H_{t}) the canonical coordinate variables. Write QH,μηQ_{H,\mu}^{\eta} for the law on (ΩH,ℋ)(\Omega_{H},\mathcal{H}) of a historical Brownian DW process, with branching rate one, with bounded measurable annihilation/creation rate η:Rd→R\eta:R^{d}\to R, and with initial condition μ∈MF​(Rd)\mu\in M_{F}(R^{d}). Letting 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the QH,μηQ^{\eta}_{H,\mu} null sets we define a filtration by ℋt=∩s>tσ{Hr:r≤s}∨𝒩\mathcal{H}_{t}=\cap_{s>t}\sigma\{H_{r}:r\leq s\}\vee\mathcal{N}. The canonical process H=(Ht)H=(H_{t}) is a historical DW process with creation/annihilation η\eta on (ΩH,ℋ,ℋt,QH,μη)(\Omega_{H},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}_{t},Q^{\eta}_{H,\mu}). In the notation from [11], it solves the martingale problem (M​P)1,2​I,0,η^0,μ(MP)^{0,\mu}_{1,2I,0,\hat{\eta}}, where η^​(s,y)=η⁡(ys)\hat{\eta}(s,y)=\eta(y_{s}).

For (𝒞t)(\mathcal{C}_{t}) predictable C:[0,∞)×C⁡([0,∞),Rd)→RC:[0,\infty)\times C([0,\infty),R^{d})\to R, having left continuous paths of bounded variation, Theorem 2.23 of Perkins [11] constructs the integral of CC along the paths of a historical DW process as the limit (in probability, or almost surely along a subsequence)

∫0tHs​(d​Cs)=limn→∞∑i=1∞I⁡(tin<t)​Htin​(Ctin−Cti−1n),where tin=i​2n.\int^{t}_{0}H_{s}(dC_{s})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}I(t^{n}_{i}<t)H_{t^{n}_{i}}(C_{t^{n}_{i}}-C_{t^{n}_{i-1}}),\quad\mbox{where $t^{n}_{i}=i2^{n}$.} (3.23)

Note that the process ∫0tHs​(d​Cs)\int^{t}_{0}H_{s}(dC_{s}) is non-decreasing whenever CsC_{s} is also non-decreasing.

Fix a bounded domain DD and define τ=τ⁡(y)=inf{t≥0:yt∉D}\tau=\tau(y)=\inf\{t\geq 0:y_{t}\not\in D\} for y∈C⁡([0,∞),Rd)y\in C([0,\infty),R^{d}), and where inf{∅}=0\inf\{\emptyset\}=0. Define a measure ut​(d​x)u_{t}(dx) on DD by

3.2 Existence and uniqueness via change of measure

The regularity of U⁡(s,t,x)U(s,t,x) will imply that (2.2) holds, namely for all bounded measurable ϕ\phi

(Vt,ϕ)=(f,ϕ)−∫0tUs​(Vs​ϕ)​𝑑s,Qμ,fD,β,γ a.s.(V_{t},\phi)=(f,\phi)-\int^{t}_{0}U_{s}(V_{s}\phi)ds,\quad\mbox{$Q_{\mu,f}^{D,\beta,\gamma}$ a.s.} (3.39)

This would be trivial, by the fundamental theorem of calculus, were Us​(d​x)U_{s}(dx) to have continuous density in (s,x)(s,x). We show at the end of this section that it follows in our more singular setting. This completes the proof of part (i) of Theorem 2.

To show uniqueness of solutions, we take a solution (u,v)(u,v) to (1.1) on DD, on a filtered space (Ω,(ℱt),ℱ,P)(\Omega,(\mathcal{F}_{t}),\mathcal{F},P), with an arbitrary ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} measurable starting condition. A similar argument leads to the following lemma, which shows that either certain death or possible life must occur, for each pair of parameter values β,γ\beta,\gamma.

≤\displaystyle\leq β2​∫0t∫Ae−2​U[0,s]​(x)​Us​(𝑑x)​𝑑s\displaystyle\beta^{2}\int^{t}_{0}\int_{A}e^{-2U_{[0,s]}(x)}U_{s}(dx)ds
=\displaystyle= β22​∫A(1−e−2​U[0,t]​(x))​𝑑x≤β22​|A|.\displaystyle\frac{\beta^{2}}{2}\int_{A}\left(1-e^{-2U_{[0,t]}(x)}\right)dx\leq\frac{\beta^{2}}{2}|A|.

The exponential martingale is therefore uniformly integrable which establishes the claim.

Step 2: A result of Evans and Perkins [6] shows that, for any fixed t>0t>0, the laws QμD,0[Ut∈⋅]Q^{D,0}_{\mu}[U_{t}\in\cdot] and Qμ~D,0[Ut∈⋅]Q^{D,0}_{\tilde{\mu}}[U_{t}\in\cdot] of two DW(Rd,0R^{d},0) processes started at non-zero μ,μ~\mu,\,\tilde{\mu} are mutually absolutely continuous on ℳ⁡(Rd)\mathcal{M}(R^{d}). by the Markov property at time t0>0t_{0}>0. By the compact support property of solutions, f​exp⁡(−U⁡(0,t0))f\exp(-U(0,t_{0})) is identically one outside a compact set, almost surely. So, using step one,

=\displaystyle= ∫ℳ⁡(Rd)Qν,1Rd,β,γ[Ut≠0for all t]Qμ,1Rd,β,γ[Ut0∈dν].\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{M}(R^{d})}Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\nu,1}[U_{t}\neq 0\;\mbox{for all $t$}]\,Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,1}[U_{t_{0}}\in d\nu].

To remove the restrictions that μ,μ~\mu,\tilde{\mu} be compactly supported, recall that the solutions are compactly supported at any time t>0t>0 almost surely. Hence, if solutions may live from some general μ≠0\mu\neq 0, they may, by applying the Markov property at time t>0t>0, live from some, and hence all, non-zero compactly supported initial conditions. Any solution started at non-zero μ~\tilde{\mu} will have positive probability of being alive and compactly supported at small times t>0t>0 (use the continuity of the total mass process) and hence, by the Markov property again, may live for all time. ∎

The next two lemmas give a characterization of certain death, which allows us to reduce the question of possible life/certain death to the study of the total exit measures solutions on bounded domains. The existence of a non-decreasing critical curve follows from this, since these exit measures are stochastically monotone in β,γ\beta,\gamma.

Lemma 11.

Suppose μ∈ℳ⁡(Rd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(R^{d}) is compactly supported. Then Qμ,fRd,β,γQ^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,f} almost surely

Applying the first and second moment bounds (3.12,3.13), and the simple estimate P[Z>0]≥(E[Z])2/E[Z2]P[Z>0]\geq(E[Z])^{2}/E[Z^{2}] for a non-negative variable ZZ, we may find ϵ1>0\epsilon_{1}>0, depending only L,β,γL,\beta,\gamma, so that Qμ,fD,β,γ[U1(DLc)>0]≥ϵ1Q^{D,\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,f}[U_{1}(D^{c}_{L})>0]\geq\epsilon_{1} for all f∈ℬ⁡(D,[0,1])f\in\mathcal{B}(D,[0,1]) and μ⁡(1)≥1\mu(1)\geq 1. Applying the Markov property at time tt, we obtain

Qμ,fRd,β,γ​[Ut+1​(d​x)=0 or Ut+1​(DLc)>0|𝒰t]≥ϵ1∧ϵ2.Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,f}\left[\mbox{$U_{t+1}(dx)=0$ or $U_{t+1}(D_{L}^{c})>0$}\,|\,\mathcal{U}_{t}\right]\geq\epsilon_{1}\wedge\epsilon_{2}.

Lemma 12.

Suppose μ∈ℳ\mu\in\mathcal{M} is compactly supported in DD. Then

Qμ,1Rd,β,γ[U[0,∞)(Dc)=0]=Qμ,1D,β,γ[U∞∂D=0].Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,1}\left[U_{[0,\infty)}(D^{c})=0\right]=Q^{D,\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,1}[U^{\partial D}_{\infty}=0].

completing the proof. ∎

Using the above results and the comparison results stated in section 2.2 we will now deduce the existence of an non-decreasing critical curve Ψ\Psi as in Theorem 1.

Corollary 13.

There exists an non-decreasing function Ψ⁡(β):[0,∞)→[0,∞]\Psi(\beta):[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty] so that for 0≤γ<Ψ⁡(β)0\leq\gamma<\Psi(\beta) possible life occurs and for γ>Ψ⁡(β)\gamma>\Psi(\beta) certain death occurs.

Proof. Lemmas 10, 11 and 12 show, for μ≠0\mu\neq 0, that Qμ,1Rd,β,γ[Ut=0for large t≥0]=1Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,1}[U_{t}=0\;\mbox{for large $t\geq 0$}]=1 if and only if Qδ0,1Rd,β,γ[Ut=0for large t≥0]=1Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\delta_{0},1}[U_{t}=0\;\mbox{for large $t\geq 0$}]=1 if and only if Qδ0,1Rd,β,γ​[U[0,∞)​is compactly supported]=1Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\delta_{0},1}[U_{[0,\infty)}\;\mbox{is compactly supported}]=1 if and only if

supnQδ0,1Dn,β,γ[U∞∂Dn=0]=1.\sup_{n}Q^{D_{n},\beta,\gamma}_{\delta_{0},1}[U^{\partial D_{n}}_{\infty}=0]=1.

But Lemma 5 shows that these probabilities are non-increasing in β\beta and non-decreasing in γ\gamma. The result follows by setting Ψ(β)=sup{γ≥0:supnQδ0,1Dn,β,γ[U∞∂Dn=0]<1}\Psi(\beta)=\sup\{\gamma\geq 0:\sup_{n}Q^{D_{n},\beta,\gamma}_{\delta_{0},1}[U^{\partial D_{n}}_{\infty}=0]<1\}. ∎

Remark. The change of measure (3.38) can be used to show that (β,γ)→Qμ,1D,β,γ[U∞∂D=0](\beta,\gamma)\to Q^{D,\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,1}[U^{\partial D}_{\infty}=0] is continuous when DD is bounded, and hence that Qμ,1Rd,β,γ​[Ut=0 for large t]Q^{R^{d},\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,1}[\mbox{$U_{t}=0$ for large $t$}] is lower semicontinuous in β,γ\beta,\gamma. This does not seem to have any immediate implications for the continuity of Ψ\Psi.

4 Approximations

The proof of the decomposition results in section 2.2 is rather clear for particle systems that approximate our reaction diffusion system. Our first proofs used a full particle approximation with population and nutrient particles living on discrete lattices. We later realized that the key to establishing the comparisons was to discretise the effect of the nutrient, and we here present an approximation where the reaction with the nutrient occurs in a finite number of discrete ‘packages’ but the population still evolves as a continuum SPDE. This intermediate approximation makes passage to the limit easier to establish. This passage to the limit is broadly similar to many in the literature, and the points of most interest are perhaps (i) that the nutrient interaction is singular as a function of the population measure uu, and requires tightness of the occupation densities; (ii) that convergence of the exit measures follows quite simply from convergence of the population measures, via the extended martingale problem (2.4).

4.1 Construction of the approximation

The approximations will depend on a parameter NN, which we will suppress in the notation in this section. Fix a domain D⊆RdD\subseteq R^{d} and partition it as a disjoint union of sets D=∪DjD=\cup D_{j}, where each set DjD_{j} has diameter at most N−1N^{-1}. Choose a finite number of functions (ψk:1≤k≤K)(\psi_{k}:1\leq k\leq K), each of the form N−1​I​(x∈Dj)N^{-1}I(x\in D_{j}) for some DjD_{j} in the partition. Each ψk\psi_{k} will represent a small package of nutrient which may be triggered to produce new population. The function f=∑kψk≤1f=\sum_{k}\psi_{k}\leq 1 will be our approximation to the initial nutrient level.

Choose a probability space equipped with the following independent families: an i.i.d. family of rate one exponential variables eke_{k} for k≥1k\geq 1; independent DW(D,γD,\gamma) processes (uk,t:t≥0)(u_{k,t}:t\geq 0), for k≥0k\geq 0, with initial conditions

u0,0=μ,anduk,0=β​ψk​(x)​d​x​for k≥1.u_{0,0}=\mu,\quad\mbox{and}\quad u_{k,0}=\beta\psi_{k}(x)dx\;\;\mbox{for $k\geq 1$.}

Let (uk,t∂D:t≥0)(u^{\partial D}_{k,t}:t\geq 0) be the associated exit measures processes. Given realizations of these variables, the approximation can be constructed pathwise. We will list as 𝒮t⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\} the labels of those nutrient packages that have been triggered by time tt, and denote by τk∈[0,∞]\tau_{k}\in[0,\infty] the time at which the kkth nutrient package is triggered. Thus 𝒮0=∅\mathcal{S}_{0}=\emptyset and 𝒮t={k:τk≤t}\mathcal{S}_{t}=\{k:\tau_{k}\leq t\}. The approximation will satisfy

ut=u0,t+∑k∈𝒮tuk,t−τk,ut∂D=u0,t∂D+∑k∈𝒮tuk,t−τk∂D,vt=∑k∉𝒮tψk.u_{t}=u_{0,t}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}u_{k,t-\tau_{k}},\quad u^{\partial D}_{t}=u^{\partial D}_{0,t}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}u^{\partial D}_{k,t-\tau_{k}},\quad v_{t}=\sum_{k\not\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\psi_{k}. (4.1)

Moreover we want the approximation process to be triggered in such a way that

τk=inf{t:u[0,t]​(ψ^k)>ek}for k≥1\tau_{k}=\inf\left\{t:u_{[0,t]}(\hat{\psi}_{k})>e_{k}\right\}\quad\mbox{for $k\geq 1$}

where ψ^k=ψk/⟨ψk,1⟩\hat{\psi}_{k}=\psi_{k}/\langle\psi_{k},1\rangle. This uniquely specifies a process, which can be constructed pathwise by defining the triggering times τk\tau_{k} and the processes ut,vtu_{t},v_{t} inductively over the intervals between triggers (and where, on a null set, packages may be simultaneously triggered).

We now derive a martingale problem for the approximation. On the intervals [τk,τk+1)[\tau_{k},\tau_{k+1}) the approximation process evolves as a finite sum of DW processes. So it satisfies the following martingale problem: for ϕ∈Cb2​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{b}(\overline{D})

4.2 Tightness of the approximations

To pass to the limit in the martingale problems for the approximation we require tightness estimates. We tried deriving these from known tightness estimates for each of the DW processes used as building blocks, however the random start times caused some difficulties in combining the estimates, so we proceed by repeating Sugitani’s estimates for our discretized approximation.

We now include the dependence on NN and write the approximation constructed in section 4.1 as (u(N),v(N))(u^{(N)},v^{(N)}).

Proposition 14.

Let DD be a bounded domain. Suppose the approximation (u(N),v(N))(u^{(N)},v^{(N)}) has initial conditions u0(N)=μ(N)u^{(N)}_{0}=\mu^{(N)} and v0(N)=f(N)≤1v^{(N)}_{0}=f^{(N)}\leq 1 satisfying that μ(N)→μ\mu^{(N)}\to\mu weakly and f(N)→ff^{(N)}\to f in L1​(D)L^{1}(D) for some f∈ℬ⁡(D,[0,1])f\in\mathcal{B}(D,[0,1]). Then

  1. (i)

    the laws of (u(N))(u^{(N)}) are tight in D⁡([0,∞),ℳ⁡(D))D([0,\infty),\mathcal{M}(D)) and limit points are continuous,

  2. (ii)

    for any δ>0\delta>0, the laws of the occupation densities (u(N)(δ,t+δ,x):t≥0,x∈D)(u^{(N)}(\delta,t+\delta,x):t\geq 0,x\in D) are tight in C⁡([0,∞),C⁡(D))C([0,\infty),C(D))

where C⁡(D)C(D) is the space of continuous functions with the topology of uniform convergence on compacts.

Proof. The moment bound (4.7) allows us the uniform control on total mass moments:

E⁡[supt≤T|ut(N)​(1)|p]≤C⁡(p,T,β,γ)​(1+(μ(N)​(1))p).E\left[\sup_{t\leq T}|u^{(N)}_{t}(1)|^{p}\right]\leq C(p,T,\beta,\gamma)\left(1+(\mu^{(N)}(1))^{p}\right). (4.11)

To control the moments of the approximate densities, the following simple upper bound for u(N)u^{(N)} is useful. Triggering all the nutrient packages (uk:1≤k≤KN)(u_{k}:1\leq k\leq K_{N}) used in the construction of u(N)u^{(N)} at time zero gives the process u~t(N)=∑k=0KNuk,t\tilde{u}^{(N)}_{t}=\sum_{k=0}^{K_{N}}u_{k,t}. This satisfies

u(N)​(0,t,x)≤u~(N)​(0,t,x)for all x∈D and t≥0.u^{(N)}(0,t,x)\leq\tilde{u}^{(N)}(0,t,x)\quad\mbox{for all $x\in D$ and $t\geq 0$.} (4.12)

Moroever u~(N)\tilde{u}^{(N)} has the law Qμ(N)+β​f(N)​d​xD,γQ^{D,\gamma}_{\mu^{(N)}+\beta f^{(N)}dx} of a DW(D,γD,\gamma) process.

Now fix ϕ∈C02​(D¯)\phi\in C^{2}_{0}(\overline{D}). Using the decomposition (4.5), we consider the increment |ut(N)​(ϕ)−us(N)​(ϕ)||u^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)-u^{(N)}_{s}(\phi)| for 0≤s<t0\leq s<t. This leads, via the total mass moment bounds and Burkholder’s inequality, to the estimate

E⁡[supr∈[s,t]|ur(N)​(ϕ)−us(N)​(ϕ)|p]≤C⁡(|t−s|p/2+N−(d+1)​p)for all N and s,t∈[0,T],E\left[\sup_{r\in[s,t]}\left|u^{(N)}_{r}(\phi)-u^{(N)}_{s}(\phi)\right|^{p}\right]\leq C\left(|t-s|^{p/2}+N^{-(d+1)p}\right)\quad\mbox{for all $N$ and $s,t\in[0,T]$,} (4.13)

where C<∞C<\infty depends only on β,γ,ϕ,p,T\beta,\gamma,\phi,p,T and supNμ(N)​(1)\sup_{N}\mu^{(N)}(1) (we suppress this dependence below). The term N−(d+1)​pN^{-(d+1)p} comes from the size of the jumps in the Burkholder inequality, for a cadlag martingale MM, in the form E⁡[sups≤t|Ms|p]≤Cp​E​[[M]tp/2]+Cp​E​[sups≤t|Ds​M|p]E[\sup_{s\leq t}|M_{s}|^{p}]\leq C_{p}E[[M]_{t}^{p/2}]+C_{p}E[\sup_{s\leq t}|D_{s}M|^{p}]. The estimate (4.13) gives, via a Chebychev inequality,

P[sups∈[t,t+N−(d+1)]|us(N)(ϕ)−ut(N)(ϕ)|≥N−1/2]≤CN−dp/2.P\left[\sup_{s\in[t,t+N^{-(d+1)}]}\left|u^{(N)}_{s}(\phi)-u^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)\right|\geq N^{-1/2}\right]\leq CN^{-dp/2}.

By summing over the grid tj=j​N−(d+1)t_{j}=jN^{-(d+1)} and applying Borel Cantelli, we find that

|us(N)(ϕ)−ut(N)(ϕ)|≤2N−1/2 whenever 0≤s,t≤T and |s−t|≤N−(d+1), for all large N, P a.s.\left|u^{(N)}_{s}(\phi)-u^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)\right|\leq 2N^{-1/2}\quad\mbox{ whenever $0\leq s,t\leq T$ and $|s-t|\leq N^{-(d+1)}$, for all large $N$, $P$ a.s.} (4.14)

We claim that (4.13) is sufficient to imply that u(N)​(ϕ)u^{(N)}(\phi) is tight in D⁡([0,∞),R)D([0,\infty),R) and has continuous limit points. To see this we smooth the sample paths by setting u¯t(N)=Nd+1​u[t,t+N−(d+1)](N)\overline{u}^{(N)}_{t}=N^{d+1}u^{(N)}_{[t,t+N^{-(d+1)}]}. Then t→u¯(N)​(ϕ)t\to\overline{u}^{(N)}(\phi) is continuous and

|u¯t(N)​(ϕ)−u¯t(N)​(ϕ)|≤2​N(d+1)​|t−s|​‖ϕ‖∞​supr≤T+1ur(N)​(1)for all N and s,t∈[0,T].\left|\overline{u}^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)-\overline{u}^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)\right|\leq 2N^{(d+1)}|t-s|\|\phi\|_{\infty}\sup_{r\leq T+1}u^{(N)}_{r}(1)\quad\mbox{for all $N$ and $s,t\in[0,T]$.}

This together with (4.13) implies that E⁡[|u¯t(N)​(ϕ)−u¯s(N)​(ϕ)|p]≤C​|t−s|p/2E[|\overline{u}^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)-\overline{u}^{(N)}_{s}(\phi)|^{p}]\leq C|t-s|^{p/2} for s,t∈[0,T]s,t\in[0,T]. Hence the laws of u¯(N)​(ϕ)\overline{u}^{(N)}(\phi) are tight in C⁡([0,T],R)C([0,T],R). But (4.14) shows that the error supt≤T|ut(N)​(ϕ)−u¯t(N)​(ϕ)|→0\sup_{t\leq T}|u^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)-\overline{u}^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)|\to 0 almost surely and ut(N)​(ϕ)u^{(N)}_{t}(\phi) has the the same continuous limit points as u¯t(N)​(ϕ)\overline{u}^{(N)}_{t}(\phi).

Xt​(N,ϕ)=ut(N)​(ϕ)−μ(N)​(GtD​ϕ)andX¯t​(N,ϕ)=Nd+1​∫tt+N−(d+1)Xs​(N,ϕ)​𝑑s.X_{t}(N,\phi)=u^{(N)}_{t}(\phi)-\mu^{(N)}(G^{D}_{t}\phi)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\overline{X}_{t}(N,\phi)=N^{d+1}\int_{t}^{t+N^{-(d+1)}}X_{s}(N,\phi)ds.

4.3 Passage to the limit

The aim now is to prove Theorem 15 below, showing that the approximations constructed in section 4.1 converge in law to solutions of (1.1). The method is to pass to the limit in the approximate martingale problem (4.5) and confirm that any limit point of the sequence of approximations must be a solution to (1.1). Many steps in the argument are quite standard (see, for example, the arguments in Proposition II.4.2 in [10]), so we concentrate on those that concern the interaction term and the exit measures.

Since we wish to let N→∞N\to\infty, we again include this dependence in the notation. Assume the hypotheses of the tightness Proposition 14. For any subsequence, we may choose a sub-subsequence where the approximations and their occupation densities converge in distribution. By a Skorokhod embedding, we may choose versions of these approximations that converge almost surely. Without changing notation for the version and labelling the convergent sub-subsequence still as NN, we may suppose there exists a limit process uu, with continuous paths in ℳ⁡(D)\mathcal{M}(D) and a continuous field (u(s,t,x):0<s≤t,x∈D)(u(s,t,x):0<s\leq t,x\in D) so that, almost surely,

sups≤t|us(N)​(ϕ)−us​(ϕ)|→0,\displaystyle\sup_{s\leq t}\left|u^{(N)}_{s}(\phi)-u_{s}(\phi)\right|\to 0, for all ϕ∈Cb0​(D¯)\phi\in C^{0}_{b}(\overline{D}) and t<∞t<\infty, (4.24)
supx∈A,s∈[δ,t]|u(N)​(δ,s,x)−u⁡(δ,s,x)|→0,\displaystyle\sup_{x\in A,s\in[\delta,t]}\left|u^{(N)}(\delta,s,x)-u(\delta,s,x)\right|\to 0, for all 0<δ≤t<∞0<\delta\leq t<\infty and compact A⊆DA\subseteq D. (4.25)

5 Proof of the decomposition results

This section contains the proofs of the decomposition results stated in section 2.2. In section 5.1 we show that the exit and occupation measures of the approximate discrete nutrient process, as constructed in section 4.1, can be done in two stages. In section 5.2, five different examples of this two-stage construction lead to five decomposition results for the approximation processes. Passage to the limit is done in section 5.3.

5.1 A two-stage construction of the approximations

The construction of the approximation process given in section 4.1 is a pathwise construction. The approximation is constructed as a deterministic procedure, which we call the basic construction, applied to fixed realizations of the non-interacting DW(D,γD,\gamma) processes (uk:k=0,1,…)(u_{k}:k=0,1,\ldots) and exponential variables (ek:k=1,2,…)(e_{k}:k=1,2,\ldots). In this section we show that the occupation and exit measures from this construction can be built up in two stages, where each stage applies the basic construction to a certain set of variables. This is described in a somewhat abstract manner, and the reader might want to look ahead at one of the five examples in section 5.2 to be convinced it is a natural idea. For the rest of this subsection we act pathwise, supposing a single realization has been fixed of the underlying variables.

Integrating over tt in (4.1), or letting t→∞t\to\infty, we obtain

u[0,∞)=u0,[0,∞)+∑k∈𝒮∞uk,[0,∞)andu∞∂D=u0,∞∂D+∑k∈𝒮∞uk,∞∂D,u_{[0,\infty)}=u_{0,[0,\infty)}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_{\infty}}u_{k,[0,\infty)}\quad\mbox{and}\quad u^{\partial D}_{\infty}=u^{\partial D}_{0,\infty}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_{\infty}}u^{\partial D}_{k,\infty}, (5.1)

where 𝒮∞=limt→∞𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{\infty}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathcal{S}_{t} is the set of labels of nutrient packages that are ever triggered. So the total occupation and exit measures are determined by the set 𝒮∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty} and the total occupation and exit measures of the non-interacting DW processes. Moreover for k∈𝒮∞k\in\mathcal{S}_{\infty} we have

u0,[0,∞)​(ψ^k)+∑j∈𝒮∞uj,[0,∞)​(ψ^k)>eku_{0,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{\infty}}u_{j,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})>e_{k}

while for the k∉𝒮∞k\not\in\mathcal{S}_{\infty} the converse inequality holds. This is exactly the condition that 𝒮∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty} is a fixed point of the mapping TT defined in the abstract lemma below, once the choices A={1,…,K}A=\{1,\ldots,K\} and

e(k)=ek,f(k)=u0,[0,∞)(ψ^k),M(j,k)=uj,[0,∞)(ψ^k)for j,k∈Ae(k)=e_{k},\quad f(k)=u_{0,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k}),\quad M(j,k)=u_{j,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})\quad\mbox{for $j,k\in A$}

have been made.

Lemma 16.

Suppose AA is a finite set, and fix e,f:A→[0,∞)e,f:A\to[0,\infty) and M:A×A→[0,∞)M:A\times A\to[0,\infty). Define, for B⊆AB\subseteq A,

T⁡(B)={a∈A:f⁡(a)+∑b∈BM⁡(b,a)>e⁡(a)}.T(B)=\left\{a\in A:f(a)+\sum_{b\in B}M(b,a)>e(a)\right\}. (5.2)

Then there is a unique smallest fixed point S⊆AS\subseteq A of TT, that is T⁡(S)=ST(S)=S and SS is contained in any other fixed point. Moreover if B⊆SB\subseteq S then Tn​(B)T^{n}(B) equals SS for large nn.

Proof. Since M⁡(a,b)≥0M(a,b)\geq 0 we see that if B⊆B′B\subseteq B^{\prime} then T⁡(B)⊆T⁡(B′)T(B)\subseteq T(B^{\prime}). So Tn​(∅)T^{n}(\emptyset) increases to a limit SS which must be a fixed point of TT. Any other fixed point S′S^{\prime} contains Tn​(∅)T^{n}(\emptyset) for all nn and hence contains SS and the uniqueness of the smallest fixed point is clear. If B⊆SB\subseteq S then Tn​(∅)⊆Tn​(B)⊆Tn​(S)=ST^{n}(\emptyset)\subseteq T^{n}(B)\subseteq T^{n}(S)=S and the result follows since Tn​(∅)=ST^{n}(\emptyset)=S for large nn. ∎

It is straightforward to check that 𝒮∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty} is the smallest fixed point of TT. Indeed, let kmk_{m} be the label of the mmth nutrient package to be triggered, and let τm\tau_{m} be the time it is triggered; then the definition of τm\tau_{m} shows, when τm<∞\tau_{m}<\infty, that km∈T⁡({k1,…,km−1})k_{m}\in T(\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{m-1}\}). Inductively, {k1,…,km}⊆Tm​(∅)\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}\}\subseteq T^{m}(\emptyset) must hold and letting m→∞m\to\infty shows that 𝒮∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty} is contained in the smallest fixed point of TT.

Example 0. To illustrate the use of this lemma, we give here the analogue of the comparison Lemma 6 for the approximation processes. Suppose that ∑k=1Lψk=f\sum_{k=1}^{L}\psi_{k}=f and ∑k=L+1Kψk=g\sum_{k=L+1}^{K}\psi_{k}=g. Now running the basic construction on the realizations of (u~0,u1,u2,…,uL)(\tilde{u}_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{L}) and the exponential variables (ek:k=1,…,L)(e_{k}:k=1,\ldots,L) we obtain an approximation process (u~,u~∂D,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{u}^{\partial D},\tilde{v}) started at μ+β​g​d​x\mu+\beta g\,dx and with initial nutrient level ff, and the triggered set 𝒮~∞\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\infty} that is the smallest fixed point of a corresponding mapping T~\tilde{T}. Moreover, for A⊆{1,…,L}A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\},

T~​(A)\displaystyle\tilde{T}(A) =\displaystyle= {k∈{1,…,L}:u~0,[0,∞)​(ψ^k)+∑j=1LI⁡(j∈A)​uj,[0,∞)​(ψ^k)>ek}\displaystyle\left\{k\in\{1,\ldots,L\}:\tilde{u}_{0,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})+\sum_{j=1}^{L}I(j\in A)u_{j,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})>e_{k}\right\}
=\displaystyle= {k∈{1,…,L}:u0,[0,∞)​(ψ^k)+∑j=1KI⁡(j∈A∪{L+1,…,K})​uj,[0,∞)​(ψ^k)>ek}\displaystyle\left\{k\in\{1,\ldots,L\}:u_{0,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})+\sum_{j=1}^{K}I(j\in A\cup\{L+1,\ldots,K\})u_{j,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})>e_{k}\right\}
=\displaystyle= T⁡(A∪{L+1,…,K})∖{L+1,…,K}.\displaystyle T(A\cup\{L+1,\ldots,K\})\setminus\{L+1,\ldots,K\}.

Choosing A=∅A=\emptyset and then iterating we find that Tn​(∅)∖{L+1,…,K}⊆T~n​(∅)T^{n}(\emptyset)\setminus\{L+1,\ldots,K\}\subseteq\tilde{T}^{n}(\emptyset) and hence, by Lemma 16, that 𝒮∞∖{L+1,…,K}⊆𝒮~∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty}\setminus\{L+1,\ldots,K\}\subseteq\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\infty}. Combining this with (5.1) shows that (u[0,∞),u∞∂D)(u_{[0,\infty)},u^{\partial D}_{\infty}) is smaller than (u~[0,∞),u~∞∂D)(\tilde{u}_{[0,\infty)},\tilde{u}^{\partial D}_{\infty}).

We now describe the two-stage procedure, which will build up the set 𝒮∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty} of triggered nutrient packages in two steps. We suppose there is a splitting of each of the DW processes (uk:k=0,…,K)(u_{k}:k=0,\ldots,K), and their exit measures, into two parts, uk−u^{-}_{k} and uk+u^{+}_{k}, each with continuous measure valued paths, and satisfying

(uk,[0,∞),uk,∞∂D)=(uk,[0,∞)−+uk,[0,∞)+,uk,∞∂D,−+uk,∞∂D,+).\left(u_{k,[0,\infty)},u^{\partial D}_{k,\infty}\right)=\left(u^{-}_{k,[0,\infty)}+u^{+}_{k,[0,\infty)},u^{\partial D,-}_{k,\infty}+u^{\partial D,+}_{k,\infty}\right). (5.3)

In stage one we apply the basic construction using the processes (uk−:k=0,1,…,K)(u^{-}_{k}:k=0,1,\ldots,K) and the exponential variables (ek:k=1,…,K)(e_{k}:k=1,\ldots,K) to create a process (u−,v−)(u^{-},v^{-}) and a set 𝒮∞−\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty} of triggered nutrient packages. In particular

u[0,∞)−=u0,[0,∞)−+∑k∈𝒮∞−uk,[0,∞)−.u^{-}_{[0,\infty)}=u^{-}_{0,[0,\infty)}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty}}u^{-}_{k,[0,\infty)}. (5.4)

We then define u^0,t=u0,t++∑k∈𝒮∞−uk,t+\hat{u}_{0,t}=u^{+}_{0,t}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty}}u^{+}_{k,t} and, for k∈{1,…,K}∖𝒮∞−k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\setminus\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty},

u^k,t=uk,tande^k=ek−u0,[0,∞)−​(ψ^k)−∑j∈𝒮∞−uj,[0,∞)−​(ψ^k).\hat{u}_{k,t}=u_{k,t}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\hat{e}_{k}=e_{k}-u^{-}_{0,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k})-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty}}u^{-}_{j,[0,\infty)}(\hat{\psi}_{k}). (5.5)

In stage two we run the basic construction on the processes u^0\hat{u}_{0} and (u^k:k∈{1,…,K}∖𝒮∞−)(\hat{u}_{k}:k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\setminus\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty}), with the nutrient packages triggered using the values (e^k:k∈{1,…,K}∖𝒮∞−)(\hat{e}_{k}:k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\setminus\mathcal{S}^{-}_{\infty}). Remark. A more natural splitting for the final example is to let (uk−,uk+)(u^{-}_{k},u^{+}_{k}) solve, for each kk, the system

∂tu−\displaystyle\partial_{t}u^{-} =\displaystyle= Δ​u−−γ−​u−+u−​W˙−,\displaystyle\Delta u^{-}-\gamma^{-}u^{-}+\sqrt{u^{-}}\,\dot{W}^{-},
∂tu+\displaystyle\partial_{t}u^{+} =\displaystyle= Δ​u++γ+​u−−γ​u++u+​W˙+,\displaystyle\Delta u^{+}+\gamma^{+}u^{-}-\gamma u^{+}+\sqrt{u^{+}}\,\dot{W}^{+},

with u0+=0u^{+}_{0}=0 and with orthogonal martingale terms. Then uk−u^{-}_{k} is a DW(D,γ−D,\gamma-) process and uk=uk−+uk+u_{k}=u_{k}^{-}+u_{k}^{+} is a DW(D,γD,\gamma) process. The first stage of the construction produces a process (u−,v−)(u^{-},v^{-}) with law Qμ,fN,D,β,γ−Q^{N,D,\beta,\gamma^{-}}_{\mu,f}. The second stage produces a process (u+,v+)(u^{+},v^{+}) which, conditional on 𝒢−\mathcal{G}^{-}, has the law of the approximation process with parameters β,γ\beta,\gamma, but with an extra immigration term γ+​u−\gamma^{+}u^{-}. This leads to a corresponding decomposition for solutions with immigration to (1.1), but we shall not make any use of it.

5.3 Completion of the proof of the comparison results

This section contains the proofs of the decomposition lemmas 4, 5, 6 and 7, using the comparison results for the approximations from section 5.2 with the convergence of the approximations established in section 5.1.

We start with a simple estimate controlling the death time τ=inf{t:Ut=0}\tau=\inf\{t:U_{t}=0\} for the approximation processes on a bounded domain uniformly in NN. The change of measure argument given at the beginning of section 3.3 can be used to show the limiting death time has a tail Qμ,fD,β,γ[τ≥t]≤C(β,p,|D|,μ)t−pQ^{D,\beta,\gamma}_{\mu,f}[\tau\geq t]\leq C(\beta,p,|D|,\mu)t^{-p} for any p<1p<1. This argument does not apply directly to the approximations since they are not absolutely continuous with respect to a DW process. However, the argument below follows the same main idea. It is combined with a first moment argument that leads to a suboptimal bound, but which is sufficient for our needs.

{∂tu=Δ​u+θ​u−u​v+u​W˙,∂tv=u,v0=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u+\theta u-uv+\sqrt{u}\,\dot{W},\\ \partial_{t}v=u,\quad v_{0}=0.\end{array}\right. (6.8)

There is monotonicity of total occupation and exit measures in θ\theta and one expects that there is a critical θc\theta_{c} so that solutions to (6.8) die for θ<θc\theta<\theta_{c} and may live for θ>θc\theta>\theta_{c}. It is therefore reasonable to conjecture that limβ→∞β−2/(6−d)(β−Ψ(β))=θc\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\beta^{-2/(6-d)}(\beta-\Psi(\beta))=\theta_{c}. There is no obvious line of proof for this conjecture, since it is not obvious that a life or death block estimate will hold for θ\theta close to θc\theta_{c}. However note that the block construction we have presented in section 6.2 uses initial nutrient condition f=I⁡(x1≥0)f=I(x_{1}\geq 0), and the above intuition does not apply as such. One needs a more careful block construction where the nutrient level is controlled, and this in turn seems to require a stronger version of the spatial Markov property. We will present these details in a subsequent paper.

We remark that a similar one parameter scaling limit should hold for the small β\beta asymptotic. Indeed letting β→0\beta\to 0 in (6.3) suggest that the small β\beta behaviour when γ=L−2​β2\gamma=L^{-2}\beta^{2} should approximate the one parameter system

The analogous conjecture is that that this equation makes sense, that it has has a critical value LcL_{c}, and that the limit Ψ⁡(β)/β2\Psi(\beta)/\beta^{2} exists and equals LcL_{c}.

Remark The approach above can be applied to the case of d=2d=2 and small β\beta. An analysis of the first moment shows that when γ=exp(−C/β)\gamma=\exp(-C/\beta) the above series construction converges for suitable CC and hence certain death. We do not include the details since the argument is quite crude and it seems easier to conjecture that there is death when γ=0\gamma=0 for small β\beta. Note however that when γ=0\gamma=0 a first moment argument will not show death since the first moment Qμ,1DR,β,0​[U∞∂DR​(1)]→∞Q^{D_{R},\beta,0}_{\mu,1}[U^{\partial D_{R}}_{\infty}(1)]\to\infty as R→∞R\to\infty. We hope to comment on this in a subsequent paper.
